title: Resources
text:
Definitions from Glosario
Further definitions at Glosario
Argument: one of possibly several expressions that are passed to a function. Oftentimes parameter and arugument are used interchangably, even though techincally parameter refers to the variable and argument refers to the value.
Assignment operator: Symbol that assigns values on the right to an object on the left. Looks like <-. Keyboard shortcut is Alt + -
Comment: Text written in a script that is not treated as code to be run, but rather as text that describes what the code is doing. These are usually short notes, beginning with a #
Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN): A public repository of R packages.
Data frame: A two-dimensional data structure for storing tabular data in memory. Rows represent records and columns represent variables.
Function: A code block which gathers a sequence of operations into a whole, preserving it for ongoing use by defining a set of tasks that takes zero or more required and optional arguments as inputs and returns expected outputs (return values), if any. Functions enable repeating these defined tasks with one command, known as a function call.
NA: A special value used to represent data that is not available.
Pipe operator: The %>% used to make the output of one function the input of the next.
Package: A collection of code, data, and documentation that can be distributed and re-used. Also referred to in some languages as a library or module.
Parameter: A variable specified in a function definition whose value is passed to the function when the function is called. Parameters and arguments are distinct, but related concepts. Parameters are variables and arguments are the values assigned to those variables. In practice though these terms are often used interchangeably.
Positional argument: An argument to a function that gets its value according to its place in the function’s definition, as opposed to a named argument that is explicitly matched by name.
Reproducible research: The practice of describing and documenting research results in such a way that another researcher or person can re-run the analysis code on the same data to obtain the same result.
Tibble: A modern replacement for R’s data frame, which stores tabular data in columns and rows, defined and used in the tidyverse. Almost always when you are working with a data frame, you are actually working with a tibble.
Tidy data: Tabular data that satisfies three conditions that facilitate initial cleaning, and later exploration and analysis—(1) each variable forms a column, (2) each observation forms a row, and (3) each type of observation unit forms a table.
Tidyverse: A collection of R packages for operating on tabular data in consistent ways.
Variable: A name in a program that has some data associated with it. A variable’s value can be changed after definition.
Vector: A sequence of values that have all the same type. Vectors are the fundamental data structure in R; a scalar is just a vector with exactly one element.

title: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups and HIV status in Botswana
text: Work a real dataset end-to-end: from a sequencing-derived haplogroup call to a hypothesis test — and to the reason the hypothesis test cannot be trusted.
crumbs: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups & HIV status

title: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups and HIV status in Botswana
text:
Why this module
Every dataset you have analysed so far in this series was chosen because it behaves. This one does not. It is a real study: 338 participants from Botswana, mitochondrial genomes sequenced, haplogroups assigned with HaploGrep 3, and paired with HIV status.
The scientific question was simple: does mitochondrial ancestry associate with HIV status?
The answer turns out to be “we cannot tell from this data” — and finding out why is the actual lesson. Learning to recognise that situation is worth more than another clean p-value.
crumbs: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups & HIV status

title: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups and HIV status in Botswana
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this module you should be able to:

Load and inspect a real haplogroup dataset with the tidyverse.
Derive a coarser grouping (macro-haplogroup) from a fine-grained label.
Build and interpret a contingency table.
Choose between a chi-squared and a Fisher exact test, and know why.
Detect confounding before you believe a result.
crumbs: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups & HIV status

title: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups and HIV status in Botswana
text:
The data






ImportantThis is a synthetic teaching dataset



The real Botswana cohort is not distributed with this workshop — it carries participant HIV status and stays private. The block below regenerates a synthetic dataset with the same shape (338 participants, L-lineage haplogroups) and, crucially, the same fatal design flaw: sex perfectly confounded with HIV status. Every number on this page comes from that synthetic data. Do not cite any of it as a real epidemiological result.



set.seed(1)
n <- 338

# Macro-haplogroups: L0 dominant, L1 rare — as in the real Southern African cohort
macro <- sample(c("L0", "L1", "L2", "L3"), n, replace = TRUE,
                prob = c(0.53, 0.05, 0.16, 0.24))

# Fine-grained labels, long-tailed so most have only a handful of carriers
sub_pool <- c("a1","a1b","a1b1","a2","a2a","a2a1","a2a2","a2a2a","b1","b2",
              "b2a","b2b","c","c1","d","d1","d1a","d1b","d1b1","d1b2",
              "d1b2b","d1b2b1","d1b2b1b","d3","d3a","d3b","e","e1","e1a",
              "e1a1","e1a1a","f","f1","f1a","f1b","f1b1","g1","h","h1","k1a")
haplogroup <- paste0(macro,
  sample(sub_pool, n, replace = TRUE, prob = rev(seq_along(sub_pool))^1.3))

# The sampling artifact: every man entered through the HIV-negative arm, so the
# HIV-positive group is women only. HIV status is otherwise independent of
# haplogroup — there is no real haplogroup effect built in.
sex <- sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.88, 0.12))
hiv_status <- ifelse(sex == "M", "negative",
                     sample(c("positive", "negative"), n,
                            replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.75, 0.25)))

mtdna <- tibble(
  participant_id   = sprintf("BW_%04d", sample(n)),
  haplogroup       = haplogroup,
  macro_haplogroup = macro,
  sex              = sex,
  hiv_status       = hiv_status
)
glimpse(mtdna)

Rows: 338
Columns: 5
$ participant_id   <chr> "BW_0331", "BW_0084", "BW_0329", "BW_0175", "BW_0013"…
$ haplogroup       <chr> "L0c", "L0f", "L3f1b", "L2a2", "L0b2b", "L2a2a2a", "L…
$ macro_haplogroup <chr> "L0", "L0", "L3", "L2", "L0", "L2", "L2", "L3", "L3",…
$ sex              <chr> "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F", "F"…
$ hiv_status       <chr> "positive", "negative", "negative", "positive", "posi…


Five columns:



Column
Meaning




participant_id
De-identified participant code


haplogroup
Full HaploGrep 3 call, e.g. L0d1b2b1b


macro_haplogroup
First two characters, e.g. L0


sex
Recorded sex


hiv_status
positive / negative









NoteWhere macro_haplogroup comes from



Haplogroup labels are hierarchical: L0d1b2b1b sits inside L0d1b2, inside L0d, inside L0. Truncating to two characters collapses the 97 fine-grained labels here into 4 macro-groups. We do this because most of those labels have only a handful of participants — far too few to test.

title: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups and HIV status in Botswana
text:
Step 1 — Look before you test

mtdna |> count(macro_haplogroup, sort = TRUE)

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  macro_haplogroup     n
  <chr>            <int>
1 L0                 197
2 L3                  78
3 L2                  48
4 L1                  15


Four macro-haplogroups, all within the L lineage — as expected for a Southern African cohort. L0 dominates, which is consistent with L0 being the deepest branch of the human mtDNA tree and common in Khoe-San-related ancestry.

mtdna |>
  count(macro_haplogroup) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(macro_haplogroup, -n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4C72B0") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = "Macro-haplogroup", y = "Participants",
       title = "mtDNA macro-haplogroup distribution (n = 338)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
crumbs: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups & HIV status

title: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups and HIV status in Botswana
text:
Step 2 — The contingency table

tab <- table(mtdna$macro_haplogroup, mtdna$hiv_status)
tab

    
     negative positive
  L0       71      126
  L1        4       11
  L2       15       33
  L3       31       47


Eyeball it before testing. Roughly two-thirds of every row is positive. The rows look similar — which is already a hint about what the test will say.

mtdna |>
  ggplot(aes(x = macro_haplogroup, fill = hiv_status)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(negative = "#8FBCD4", positive = "#C44E52")) +
  labs(x = "Macro-haplogroup", y = "Proportion", fill = NULL,
       title = "HIV status within each macro-haplogroup") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
crumbs: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups & HIV status

title: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups and HIV status in Botswana
text:
Step 3 — Test it

chisq.test(tab)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  tab
X-squared = 1.5096, df = 3, p-value = 0.6801


The p-value is well above 0.05 — no evidence of association.






Tipchi-squared or Fisher?



Chi-squared is an approximation that degrades when expected cell counts fall below ~5. Check first:

chisq.test(tab)$expected |> round(1)

    
     negative positive
  L0     70.5    126.5
  L1      5.4      9.6
  L2     17.2     30.8
  L3     27.9     50.1


The L1 row is thin. Fisher’s exact test does not rely on the approximation:

fisher.test(tab, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 10000)


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data with simulated p-value (based on
    10000 replicates)

data:  tab
p-value = 0.6984
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


Both agree — no association. When two tests with different assumptions agree, you can stop worrying about which one to report.
crumbs: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups & HIV status

title: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups and HIV status in Botswana
text:
Step 4 — The part that matters
Before you write “no association between mtDNA haplogroup and HIV status” in a manuscript, run one more line:

table(mtdna$sex, mtdna$hiv_status)

   
    negative positive
  F       76      217
  M       45        0


Read that table carefully.
Every single male in this cohort is HIV-negative. Every HIV-positive participant is female.
That is not biology. No cohort in Botswana looks like this by chance — HIV prevalence in men is not zero. This is a sampling artifact: the HIV-negative comparison group was recruited in a way that pulled in the only men in the study.
The consequence is severe. Sex is perfectly confounded with HIV status, so:

Any haplogroup–HIV signal is inseparable from a haplogroup–sex signal.
You cannot adjust for sex. Adjustment needs some overlap — HIV-positive men or HIV-negative-only women to compare against. There are none.
The null result above is therefore uninformative, not reassuring. We did not find “no effect”; we found that this design cannot measure the effect.







ImportantThe transferable lesson



A p-value answers the question you asked. It cannot tell you the question was unanswerable. Always cross-tabulate your exposure against your key covariates before you interpret a test. One table() call would have saved this analysis.
Because mtDNA is maternally inherited, a sex imbalance is especially dangerous here — but this failure mode is completely general.
crumbs: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups & HIV status

title: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups and HIV status in Botswana
text:
Exercises
1. Restrict the analysis to women only and re-run the test. What is the p-value now? Does restricting fix the confounding, and what did you pay for it?

women <- mtdna |> filter(sex == "F")
# your code here

2. Collapse to L0 vs everything else and test with fisher.test(). Does a binary comparison change the conclusion?
3. The fine-grained haplogroups were collapsed to 4 macro-groups. Count participants per full haplogroup. How many have fewer than 5? What would happen to a chi-squared test run on the uncollapsed table?
4. Discussion. You are handed this dataset and asked to publish the null result. What do you tell the team, and what would you need to collect to answer the original question properly?
crumbs: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups & HIV status

title: Case study: mtDNA haplogroups and HIV status in Botswana
text:
What to take away

Real data arrives with defects that no amount of correct statistics repairs.
Look at marginals and cross-tabs before testing.
A null result from a confounded design is not a null result.
Reporting why a question cannot be answered is a legitimate scientific contribution.







NoteAbout this dataset





Synthetic. It is generated in the code block above to mirror a real study of mitochondrial genomes in Botswana — the same size, the same L-lineage haplogroup structure, and the same sex/HIV confounding that makes the real analysis uninterpretable — without using any real participant data. The real cohort is not distributed: it carries HIV status and remains private. Nothing on this page should be read as an actual result from the Botswana study.

title: Bioinformatics & Application
text:
About this section
Section 2 covered methods that learn from data. This section covers the computational pipeline that produces that data — and the artifacts it introduces at every step.
The running example is hepatitis B virus, using real sequencing data from Botswana.

title: Bioinformatics & Application
text:
The through-line






ImportantEvery step is lossy



Extraction favours some templates. PCR duplicates inflate apparent depth. Basecalling guesses. Alignment forces a read to a position that may be wrong. Variant calling applies a threshold someone chose.
By the time you have a VCF, five judgement calls stand between you and the biology. Knowing they happened is the difference between analysis and credulity.

title: Module 3: Genotyping & Recombination
text: Assigning a genotype assumes the genome has one. Recombinants do not.

title: Module 3: Genotyping & Recombination
text:
Learning objectives

Describe how HBV genotypes are defined.
Assign a genotype by similarity to references.
Explain why whole-sequence classifiers fail on recombinants.
Interpret a jpHMM breakpoint plot.

title: Module 3: Genotyping & Recombination
text:
What a genotype is
HBV genotypes (A–J) are defined by sequence divergence — historically >8% across the complete genome. Subgenotypes (A1, A2, D3…) subdivide further.
Genotype is not academic bookkeeping. It tracks with disease progression, treatment response, and geography. In Botswana, A1 and D3 dominate, which is itself an epidemiological signal.

title: Module 3: Genotyping & Recombination
text:
The naive approach
Align a query against references, take the most similar. This works, right up until it doesn’t.






ImportantThe recombination problem



A recombinant genome is genotype A across part of its length and genotype E across another. A whole-sequence classifier must return a single label. It will return one, with high confidence, and it will be wrong — the “similarity” it reports is an average over segments that disagree.
A confident answer from a method that cannot express uncertainty is the most dangerous output in bioinformatics.

title: Module 3: Genotyping & Recombination
text:
Why jpHMM is different
jpHMM (jumping profile Hidden Markov Model) does not classify the genome as a unit. It walks along the sequence, and at each position asks which genotype’s profile best explains the data — with the option to jump between genotypes.
The output is a genotype assignment per region, plus the breakpoints where it switched. For a pure genotype, one assignment spans the genome. For a recombinant, you see the mosaic directly.
This is a general lesson: the right model is the one whose structure matches the biology. Recombination is a positional process, so the model must be positional.

title: Module 3: Genotyping & Recombination
text:
Reading breakpoints skeptically
Not every reported breakpoint is real. Consider:

Low coverage. A breakpoint where depth collapses is suspect.
Short segments. A 50bp “genotype E” island inside genotype A is more likely noise than biology.
Reference bias. If the true genotype is absent from your reference set, jpHMM assigns the closest available — and may invent a mosaic to do it.







WarningMissing references manufacture recombinants



An unrepresented lineage gets explained as a patchwork of the lineages you did include. Before reporting a novel recombinant, ask whether your reference panel could represent the truth.

title: Module 3: Genotyping & Recombination
text:
Exercises

Assign genotypes to workshop sequences by similarity. Where is the call close?
Run jpHMM. Do any sequences show breakpoints?
For one breakpoint: check depth and segment length. Do you believe it?
Discussion. You find a novel A/E recombinant. What must you rule out first?

title: Module 3: Genotyping & Recombination
text:
Takeaways

Genotype assumes a single ancestry. Recombinants violate that.
Match model structure to the biology.
Suspect your reference panel before announcing a new recombinant.

title: Module 1: Sequence Data & Quality Control
text: The first rule of sequence analysis: look at your reads before you trust them.

title: Module 1: Sequence Data & Quality Control
text:
Learning objectives

Read a FASTQ record and interpret its quality line.
Convert between Phred scores and error probabilities.
Identify adapter contamination and decide what to trim.
Explain why aggressive trimming can be worse than none.

title: Module 1: Sequence Data & Quality Control
text:
The FASTQ record
Four lines per read:
@hbv_TR_R02B35_read1          <- identifier
GCTGCTATGCCTCATCTTCTTGTTGGT   <- sequence
+                             <- separator
IIIIIIIIIIIHHHHHGGGGFFFEEDD   <- quality, one char per base
Line 4 is the one people ignore. Each character encodes a Phred score:
\[Q = -10 \log_{10} P(\text{base is wrong})\]



Q
Error probability
Meaning




10
1 in 10
Poor


20
1 in 100
Acceptable


30
1 in 1,000
Good


40
1 in 10,000
Excellent









NoteThe scale is logarithmic



Q30 → Q20 is a tenfold increase in error rate, not a 33% one. Small-looking drops in mean quality matter more than they appear.

title: Module 1: Sequence Data & Quality Control
text:
What to look for

Quality by position. Quality falls toward the 3’ end on Illumina — that is normal chemistry, not a failed run.
Adapter contamination. When the insert is shorter than the read, you sequence into the adapter. These bases are real sequence, but not your sequence, and they will not align.
Duplication. PCR duplicates inflate apparent depth without adding information. Ten reads from one original molecule is not tenfold evidence.
Length distribution. For long reads, a large spread is expected.

title: Module 1: Sequence Data & Quality Control
text:
The trimming trade-off






WarningAggressive trimming causes its own problems



Trimming at Q30 discards real data and biases you toward the reference: reads carrying true variants often have slightly lower quality at the variant position, so hard filtering can systematically remove the variants you are looking for.
Trim adapters always. Trim quality gently. Q20 is usually plenty.

title: Module 1: Sequence Data & Quality Control
text:
Long reads are different
Nanopore data has higher per-base error, and it is not uniformly distributed — homopolymer runs are systematically harder. Five A’s may be called as four. This is a known failure mode and no amount of coverage fixes a systematic error.
The compensation is read length: a 3kb read spanning the whole HBV genome resolves structure that short reads cannot.

title: Module 1: Sequence Data & Quality Control
text:
Exercises

Take a FASTQ from the workshop data. What is the mean quality? Where does it drop?
Convert Q25 to an error probability by hand.
Trim at Q20 and Q30. How many reads survive each? What did Q30 cost you?
Discussion. Why might a variant caller miss a real variant in a homopolymer?

title: Module 1: Sequence Data & Quality Control
text:
Takeaways

Look at quality before analysis, every time.
Trim adapters always; trim quality gently.
Nanopore errors are systematic, not random.

text: Five modules, building from “what is a model” to “should I have used one”.

title: AI and Application
text:
About this section
Section 1 argued that method choice follows from the question. This section teaches the methods themselves — enough to use them, and enough to know when not to.
Every module uses real data. Where a method is a poor fit for the data we have, we say so rather than pretending otherwise.

How to read this section

ImportantA running theme

Prerequisites

title: Module 4: Deep Learning & Sequence Models
text: Neural networks earned their reputation on problems that look nothing like a 338-row spreadsheet.

title: Module 4: Deep Learning & Sequence Models
text:
Learning objectives

Describe what a neural network is without mystification.
Explain why deep learning needs large datasets.
Name the biological problems where it genuinely won, and why.
Decide honestly whether your problem qualifies.

title: Module 4: Deep Learning & Sequence Models
text:
What a neural network is
A stack of linear transformations with non-linear functions between them, fitted by gradient descent. That is the whole idea. “Deep” means many layers.
The power comes from learned representations: you do not hand-engineer features, the network derives them. That is also the cost — the features it learns are usually not interpretable.

title: Module 4: Deep Learning & Sequence Models
section: Why it needs so much data
text:
Why it needs so much data
Each connection is a parameter. Modern architectures have millions. Fitting millions of parameters requires enormous numbers of examples, or the network memorises.






ImportantThe scale mismatch



AlphaFold trained on ~170,000 structures. Nanopore basecallers train on billions of signal-base pairs. If you have 338 samples, you are five orders of magnitude away from this regime. Deep learning is not the tool.

title: Module 4: Deep Learning & Sequence Models
text:
Where it genuinely won







Problem
Why it worked




Protein structure
170k solved structures; clear input/output; objective metric


Basecalling
Effectively unlimited training signal


Variant effect
Large curated databases


Image analysis
Transfers from a field with millions of labelled images



The pattern: massive labelled corpora, well-defined objective, tolerance for opacity.

title: Module 4: Deep Learning & Sequence Models
text:
Sequence models
DNA is a string, so architectures from language modelling apply. Transformers handle long-range dependencies — relevant because regulatory elements act at distance.
This is genuinely promising, and mostly it means using pre-trained models, not training your own. Fine-tuning an existing model on a few hundred sequences is occasionally reasonable. Training from scratch on your cohort is not.






WarningPre-trained does not mean unbiased



Genomic models are trained overwhelmingly on European-ancestry data. Applied to African cohorts, performance can degrade in ways that are silent and systematic. For Southern African genomics this is not hypothetical — it is a live problem, and one your work is positioned to document.

title: Module 4: Deep Learning & Sequence Models
text:
The honest self-assessment

Do I have >10,000 labelled examples? If no, stop.
Do I need learned features, or do I know the mechanism?
Can I tolerate an unexplainable answer?
Has my baseline been beaten yet?

Most biological questions in this workshop fail at step 1. That is not a limitation of your science — it is a property of the method.

title: Module 4: Deep Learning & Sequence Models
text:
Exercises

Estimate the parameter count for a small network. Compare to your sample size.
Find a published deep learning genomics paper. What was n? Would it work on your cohort?
Argue the case against deep learning for a problem in your own work.

title: Module 4: Deep Learning & Sequence Models
text:
Takeaways

Neural networks are function approximators, not magic.
The data requirement is the binding constraint.
Pre-trained models carry their training data’s ancestry bias.

title: Module 2: Supervised Learning
text: You have labels. You want to extend them to new cases. This is the most common — and most over-applied — setup in biology.

title: Module 2: Supervised Learning
text:
Learning objectives

Fit and interpret a logistic regression.
Read a confusion matrix.
Explain why interpretable coefficients often beat a small accuracy gain.
Recognise when your labels, not your model, are the problem.

title: Module 2: Supervised Learning
text:
Start with regression
Logistic regression is a machine learning model. It is also interpretable, fast, and hard to overfit with few predictors. In clinical genomics that combination is difficult to beat.

fit <- glm(outcome ~ predictor1 + predictor2,
           data = train, family = binomial)
summary(fit)
exp(coef(fit))   # odds ratios

An odds ratio is something you can put in a paper and defend to a clinician.

title: Module 2: Supervised Learning
text:
The confusion matrix




Predicted +
Predicted −




Actually +
True positive
False negative


Actually −
False positive
True negative



Everything — sensitivity, specificity, precision — comes from these four numbers. Report the matrix, not just a summary statistic derived from it.






ImportantThe two errors are not equal



Missing a treatable infection is not the same as an unnecessary follow-up test. Your metric must reflect which error is worse in your setting. No default does this for you.

title: Module 2: Supervised Learning
section: How many predictors can I afford?
text:
How many predictors can I afford?
Roughly 10 events per predictor. With 40 cases you can justify about four variables. This constraint is not negotiable by using a fancier model — a flexible model with 40 events overfits harder, not less.

title: Module 2: Supervised Learning
text:
When labels are the problem
Your model inherits every bias in its labels. If severe cases were preferentially tested, “predicts disease” may really mean “predicts who got tested”.






WarningAsk how labels were assigned



Before training: who decided, using what criteria, on which patients? If labels came from a biased process, high accuracy means you reproduced the bias faithfully.

title: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method
text:
How this works
Six scenarios, all drawn from real Southern African genomics research. For each one, decide:

Is this supervised, unsupervised, generative, or not an AI problem at all?
What method would you actually use?
What could go wrong?

Question 3 is the one that matters. Work in pairs, 20 minutes, then we discuss.






TipThe most common right answer



“Not an AI problem” is correct more often than people expect. Do not talk yourself out of it.
crumbs: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method

title: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method
text:
Scenario 1 — Genotype assignment
You have 6,000 HBV sequences. For 500 of them a reference lab has assigned a genotype (A, B, C, D, E). You want genotypes for the other 5,500.

Supervised, unsupervised, generative, or not AI?
What would you use?
What could go wrong?







NoteDiscussion





Supervised — you have labels and want to extend them.
But before training anything: this is a solved problem with a known mechanism. Genotype is defined by sequence divergence, so alignment against reference genotypes (or a tool like jpHMM) is the standard approach and it is interpretable — you can point at the evidence.
What could go wrong: the 500 labelled sequences may not be a random sample. If the reference lab preferentially genotyped unusual cases, your labels are biased and the model inherits that. Recombinant sequences break everything — if a genome is part A and part E, a whole-sequence classifier must pick one and will be confidently wrong. That is precisely why jpHMM scans along the genome instead of classifying it as a unit.
crumbs: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method

title: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method
text:
Scenario 2 — Structure in haplogroups
You have 338 mtDNA haplogroup calls. Nobody has grouped them. You want to know whether the cohort contains distinct ancestry clusters.






NoteDiscussion





Unsupervised — no labels, looking for structure.
But note that haplogroups are already a hierarchical classification built by phylogenetics. Clustering them is close to re-deriving a tree that exists. The honest first move is count() and a bar chart.
What could go wrong: clustering always returns clusters. With 62 fine-grained labels over 338 people, most labels have a handful of members — you will find “structure” that is sampling noise. This dataset is used in the case study; it collapses to 4 macro-groups for exactly this reason.
crumbs: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method

title: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method
text:
Scenario 3 — Drug resistance from sequence
You have 200 sequenced isolates with known resistance phenotypes. You want to predict resistance for new isolates from sequence alone.






NoteDiscussion





Supervised — and the tempting answer is “train a classifier”.
With 200 examples and thousands of positions, you have far more features than samples. A flexible model will memorise. Start with known resistance mutations from the literature — mechanism you already have — and use regression on those positions.
What could go wrong: severe class imbalance. If 15 of 200 are resistant, a model predicting “susceptible” always is 92% accurate and clinically dangerous. And a model trained on one subtype may not transfer to another.
crumbs: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method

title: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method
section: Scenario 4 — Does haplogroup associate with HIV status?
text:
Scenario 4 — Does haplogroup associate with HIV status?
338 participants, mtDNA haplogroup and HIV status for each. Does ancestry associate with infection status?






NoteDiscussion





Not an AI problem. Four groups, one binary outcome, 338 people. This is a contingency table and Fisher’s exact test.
What could go wrong: everything — and not for statistical reasons. In the real version of this dataset, every male is HIV-negative and every HIV-positive participant is female. Sex is perfectly confounded with outcome, so no method — Fisher, regression, or a neural network — can separate a haplogroup effect from a sex effect.
The result is not “no association”. It is “this design cannot answer the question”. You would find this with one table() call and never find it by tuning a model. This is the case study.
crumbs: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method

title: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method
text:
Scenario 5 — Writing your methods section
You want an LLM to draft the methods section describing your pipeline.






NoteDiscussion





Generative — and legitimate, with conditions.
Useful for: restructuring text you wrote, tightening prose, drafting boilerplate you will verify.
What could go wrong: LLMs produce fluent, plausible, wrong text. They will invent a citation that looks perfect. They will state a version number you never used. Everything factual — versions, parameters, references — must be checked against your actual pipeline.
Also: journals require disclosure of AI assistance, and you remain responsible for every sentence. “The model wrote it” is not a defence.
crumbs: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method

title: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method
text:
Scenario 6 — Predicting who progresses
You have 50 patients with longitudinal viral load and want to predict who progresses to liver disease.






NoteDiscussion





Supervised, and the honest answer is you probably cannot do this yet.
Fifty patients, with perhaps 12 events. The rule of thumb is ~10 events per predictor, so you can justify roughly one variable. Not a model — a variable.
What could go wrong: with n=50 you can build something that looks impressive and means nothing. Informative censoring makes it worse: patients lost to follow-up may be the sickest.
The valuable contribution here is saying so — and specifying what cohort size would be needed. Telling a team their study is underpowered before they spend three years on it is worth more than any model.

title: Exercise: Match the Question to the Method
text:
Wrapping up
Across six scenarios drawn from real work:

Two were not AI problems (4, and arguably 1).
One was underpowered regardless of method (6).
One had a fatal design flaw no method could repair (4).
The failure modes were about data and design, never about algorithms.







ImportantThe point



The hard part of applying AI in biology is almost never the model. It is knowing whether the question can be answered by the data you have. That judgement is the thing this workshop is actually trying to teach.


Next: AI and Application.

title: 2. What is AI?
text: Most of what is sold as AI is a function that maps inputs to outputs, fitted on examples. That is less magical and more useful than the marketing.

title: 2. What is AI?
text:
Learning objectives

Use “AI”, “machine learning”, and “deep learning” correctly.
Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, and generative tasks.
Explain why a model that fits the training data can still be worthless.
State what a model cannot tell you, no matter how accurate it is.

title: 2. What is AI?
text:
The nesting dolls
These three words are not synonyms.
┌─ Artificial Intelligence ──────────────────────┐
│  any system that performs tasks we'd call      │
│  "intelligent" — including hand-written rules  │
│                                                │
│  ┌─ Machine Learning ───────────────────────┐  │
│  │  systems that learn patterns from data   │  │
│  │  rather than being told the rules        │  │
│  │                                          │  │
│  │  ┌─ Deep Learning ───────────────────┐   │  │
│  │  │  ML using many-layered neural     │   │  │
│  │  │  networks. Needs a lot of data.   │   │  │
│  │  └───────────────────────────────────┘   │  │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
BLAST is arguably AI — it performs an intelligent task using hand-written rules. It is definitely not machine learning: nobody trained it on examples.






TipSay what you mean



If you fitted a logistic regression, say “logistic regression”, not “we applied AI”. Reviewers notice, and precision costs you nothing.

title: 2. What is AI?
text:
The three kinds of task
Supervised — you have labelled examples and want to predict the label for new cases. This sequence is genotype A; that one is genotype D; what is this new one? Requires labels, and your model inherits every bias in them.
Unsupervised — you have no labels and want structure. Do these 338 samples fall into groups? Nothing guarantees the groups mean anything biological.
Generative — you want the model to produce new content: a protein structure, a plausible sequence, a paragraph of text. Large language models live here.




Needs labels?
Typical question
Failure mode




Supervised
Yes
“Which class?”
Learns the label’s bias


Unsupervised
No
“Is there structure?”
Finds structure in noise


Generative
Sometimes
“Make me one”
Fluent and wrong

title: 2. What is AI?
section: The one idea that matters most
text:
The one idea that matters most
A model that performs well on the data it was trained on has demonstrated nothing. It may have memorised.






ImportantOverfitting



A model with enough parameters can fit any dataset perfectly, including the noise. It will then fail on new data. The only way to know whether you have learned a pattern or memorised a table is to test on data the model has never seen.


The remedy is discipline, not cleverness: split your data before you start, hold out the test set, and do not look at it until the end. If you tune your model against the test set, it is no longer a test set.
This is not a technicality. It is the single most common reason published models fail to replicate.

title: 2. What is AI?
section: What a model cannot tell you
text:
What a model cannot tell you
An accurate model tells you two variables carry shared information. It does not tell you:

Which causes which. Correlation is symmetric; causation is not.
Whether a third thing causes both. This is confounding, and it is the subject of the hands-on case study — where a perfectly reasonable analysis produces a result that cannot be interpreted, because of how participants were recruited.
Whether the question was answerable. A model always returns a number. The number is not a judgement about your study design.







WarningAccuracy is a trap on imbalanced data



If 95% of your samples are HIV-negative, a model that predicts “negative” for everyone is 95% accurate and completely useless. Always ask what the base rate is before being impressed by an accuracy figure.

title: 2. What is AI?
text:
Check yourself

You cluster samples and find three groups. What have you learned?
Your classifier is 99% accurate on training data and 60% on held-out data. What happened?
A tool reports 95% accuracy predicting a condition affecting 5% of people. Is it good?

We work through these in the exercise.

section: Exercise 1 — SIV Integration Sites & ATAC-seq in R
text:
Exercise 1 — SIV Integration Sites & ATAC-seq in R
Session: SIV/HIV integration site profiling · 11:30 · hands-on in RStudio
Materials prepared by Aisha Olufayo (Research Intern, Boudries Lab, CVVR) — aolufayo@bidmc.harvard.edu.
You will annotate simulated SIV integration sites, then overlap them with simulated ATAC-seq peaks to ask whether the virus integrates into open chromatin.

Get the workshop files
Go to the workshop repository, click the green CODE button, then Download ZIP:
 aolufayo-bidmc/IS-ATAC-Workshop  Getting Started (PDF)
Unzip it somewhere you can find again. The package contains simulated integration site data and simulated ATAC-peak data — no participant data is involved.






NoteThis is a live repository



The code is maintained and may be updated before the session. If you downloaded the ZIP well in advance, download it again the night before so you have the current version.




Prerequisites

R — version 4.4 or later recommended
RStudio Desktop

Both are already on the Installation list for this workshop.


Install the R packages
Paste this into your R console. It checks for each package and installs only what is missing:
packages <- c("tidyverse", "readxl", "writexl", "openxlsx", "readr", "BiocManager")

for (pkg in packages) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg)
  }
}






ImportantStep 0 — do not skip this



Open the R project file IS_ATAC_Workshop_Files.Rproj first, and work from the Files pane inside that project.
This puts RStudio in the correct working directory. Filenames are written directly into the scripts for convenience, so opening the .R files any other way means the code will not find its inputs. Nearly every problem in this session traces back to this step.




The run order

2

Step 2 takes the cleaned data and annotates each insertion site: the gene it lands in, its location within that gene, the surrounding sequence.
Step 3 is the conceptual core. Both the integration sites and the ATAC-seq peaks are converted to GRanges objects, and subsetByOverlaps() finds the integration sites sharing at least one base pair with a region of open chromatin.

title: Day 2 Exercises
text:
Exercise 2 — An integration site hotspot
Session: SIV/HIV integration site profiling · 11:30 · pen and paper
Exercise 1 gave you overlaps. This one asks whether you should believe them.
You map integration sites in a real dataset and find a striking result: 31% of all sites fall in one gene, BACH2. The clonal expansion literature makes this exciting — a selected, persistently infected clone.

What would convince you this is real?
What is the alternative explanation?
What could go wrong?







NoteDiscussion





Ask what “31% of sites” is counting. If it counts sequencing reads, you have measured PCR amplification, not biology. One efficiently amplified template can dominate a library. Integration site work counts unique sites — deduplicated by breakpoint, ideally with sonication- or UMI-based fragment tagging — for exactly this reason.
The alternative explanation is the pipeline. Before biology, rule out mapping ambiguity in repetitive regions and a contaminating index-hopped sample. Then rule out the null: integration is not uniform to begin with. HIV/SIV favour actively transcribed, accessible chromatin — which is the entire premise of Exercise 1. “Found in a transcribed gene” is therefore the expectation, not the discovery.
This is why the overlap in Exercise 1 needs a control. A percentage of sites in open chromatin means nothing on its own. It only means something against a matched random control — sites shuffled while preserving whatever structure you are not testing — because comparing your observed overlap to an implicit assumption of uniformity will make even random data look enriched.
What would convince you: the same site recovered from independent samples and independent library preps; an enrichment test against that matched control; and a clone size estimated from unique breakpoints, not reads.
What could go wrong: BACH2 is a genuine, well-documented clonal expansion hotspot. That is what makes this trap effective — the literature will happily confirm a result your pipeline manufactured. A finding that matches expectation gets less scrutiny, and needs more.

title: Day 2 Exercises
text:
Exercise 3 — Reading a DESeq2 result
Session: Biomarker discovery using bulk RNA-Seq · 9:00
You run the Week 24 contrast from the bulk RNA-Seq session. Out of 18,285 genes, just over 400 come back with an adjusted p-value below 0.05. One of them looks like this:
gene      baseMean   log2FoldChange   lfcSE   padj
GENE_X       7.4          3.9          1.1    0.021

What does the sign of that fold change mean here?
Is this a biomarker candidate?
What could go wrong?







NoteDiscussion





The sign first. Status is forced to c("NoRebound", "Rebound"), so the contrast is Rebound vs NoRebound and a positive log2FoldChange means higher in Rebound. GENE_X is roughly 15-fold up in rebounders. If you got that backwards, every sentence you write about this gene is inverted.
Is it a candidate? Look at baseMean before you get excited. A mean of 7.4 counts across the samples is close to nothing — this gene is barely detected. Large fold changes are easy at low counts, because the ratio of two small noisy numbers is unstable. That is why DESeq2 shrinks fold changes, and why an lfcSE of 1.1 is telling you the estimate is soft.
What could go wrong: ranking by log2FoldChange puts low-expression noise at the top of your list. Rank by adjusted p-value, or filter on baseMean first, and look at the MA plot — the fan of large effects at the left edge is this artifact, drawn.
Also: 400 hits out of 18,285 at 5% FDR means roughly 20 are expected to be false positives. Not “the list is wrong”, but “the list contains false positives by construction, and I do not know which”.

title: Day 2 Exercises
section: Exercise 4 — GSEA and the tempting pathway
text:
Exercise 4 — GSEA and the tempting pathway
Session: Biomarker discovery using bulk RNA-Seq · 9:00
You run GSEA against the 50 MSigDB Hallmark sets. HALLMARK_INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE comes back strongly enriched in rebounders, FDR < 0.001. It is an immunologically satisfying result: interferon signalling, in a viral rebound study.

Does this tell you interferon signalling causes rebound?
What is GSEA actually testing?
What could go wrong?







NoteDiscussion





No. GSEA tests whether genes in a set sit higher in your ranked list than chance would put them. It is a statement about coordinated ranking — not mechanism, not direction of causation, not timing.
What could go wrong: several things at once.
The satisfying result is the dangerous one. Interferon response is one of the most commonly enriched Hallmark sets in any dataset involving virus, infection, or inflammation. Its appearance is weakly informative. You would have accepted it without question — which is precisely why you should question it.
Hallmark sets overlap. Genes appear in several sets, so “five enriched pathways” may be one signal counted five times. That is what the Organize_Significant_GSEA_Pathways_into_Modules.R script exists to expose.
Direction is inherited from the contrast. If you flipped the factor levels in Exercise 3, this enrichment flips with it.
Correlation with rebound is not prediction of rebound. The ML session asks the prediction question, and it is a different question with a different answer.

title: Day 2 Exercises
text:
Exercise 5 — Cells, or observations?
Session: Single cell multiome profiling in CD4 T cells · 10:15
A colleague profiles CD4 T cells from 4 SIV-infected macaques and 4 controls. After QC they have 40,000 cells. They run a differential expression test across cells, infected vs control, and report genes at p < 10⁻³⁰⁰.

Why is that p-value so small?
What is the sample size in this study?
What could go wrong?







NoteDiscussion





n = 8, not 40,000. This is pseudoreplication, and it is the single most common error in single-cell work.
Cells from one animal are not independent observations of “SIV infection”. They share that animal’s genotype, viral load, treatment history, tissue handling, and the batch it was processed in. Testing across 40,000 cells asks “do cells differ?” while the biological question is “do animals differ?” — and the test answers the question you asked, with enormous confidence, because 40,000 is a big number.
That p-value is a measure of cell count, not evidence. With enough cells you can drive any p-value arbitrarily low, including for a gene whose difference is driven entirely by one animal.
What to do instead: pseudobulk. Aggregate counts per animal per cell type, then test across the 8 animals with DESeq2 — the same tool from Exercise 3. You will get far fewer hits and far larger error bars, and that is the honest picture. Four versus four is a small study; the analysis should say so.
What could still go wrong: with n=4 per group, one outlier animal is 25% of its group. Plot per-animal values for every gene you intend to report. If the signal is one macaque, you have found one macaque.

title: Day 2 Exercises
section: Exercise 6 — Mutations, Diversity, Burden & Minority Variants
text:
Exercise 6 — Mutations, Diversity, Burden & Minority Variants
Session: Principles of Viral Evolution · 13:45 · hands-on in R
The first of the afternoon’s two practicals. You work a whole-genome HIV-1 deep-sequencing sample from raw per-position pileup all the way to minority variants, diversity, and a burden test — using real data from a single patient.

Get the practical
 Download the workshop (ZIP)  Rendered report (HTML)  Slides
The analysis is a single R Markdown document, mutations_workshop.Rmd. Open it in RStudio and run it top to bottom — every number in the prose is computed from the data, not typed in, so a clean run reproduces the whole argument.
Needs: R, RStudio, and the packages tidyverse, patchwork, knitr.






NoteThe data is real, and de-identified



This is a genuine HIV-1 sample aligned to NC_001802.1 — not a simulation. The original sample barcode has been removed from the filename and every sequence header; the pileup itself carries only positions and base counts, no identifiers. Treat it as you would any patient-derived sequence: the numbers are for learning the method, not for reporting as a clinical result.




The reversal is the point






ImportantA confident, significant result that is an artefact



Partway through, the naive minority-variant analysis — a 1% VAF threshold with a binomial test against the error rate — produces an FDR-significant result. It is wrong. It is a sequencing artefact, and the binomial test cannot see it.
You will catch it with a Ti/Tv stress test, diagnose it from the substitution spectrum, fix it by filtering the artefact signature, and then validate the fix biologically against the APOBEC3G editing signature. That catch-diagnose-fix-validate loop is the whole workshop. A p-value below your threshold is where the thinking starts, not where it ends.




What you build, in order







Section
What it covers




Dataset & QC
FASTQ-style pileup, coverage QC before any calling


What a mutation is
Consensus (ref vs strain) vs within-host variation


Types of mutation
Structural, Ti/Tv, coding effect, origin


Calculating them
Allele frequency (VAF) — and why frequency ≠ rate


Diversity
Shannon entropy per site, nucleotide diversity π, per-gene


Minority variants
The naive call, the artefact, the fix, APOBEC validation


Burden testing
Regional enrichment, then a simulated case/control cohort









NoteAn honest note carried from the workshop



A classical burden test compares cases vs controls across many individuals. This is one sample, so you cannot run one — and the document says so plainly. What you can run is the same machinery in its within-sample form (regional enrichment), then a simulated cohort for the case/control version. Being clear about what a single sample can and cannot support is itself part of the lesson.




The pol and env minority-variant sets
The ZIP also ships translated and nucleotide minority-variant FASTAs for the pol (PR, RT, IN) and env genes across a threshold sweep (5%–50%), built by pol_minority_fasta.R and env_minority_fasta.R. These feed the threshold-comparison figures and let you see how the variant set shrinks as you demand more evidence — the same “where do I set the line?” question the minority-variant section answers for the whole genome.

The main practical for the afternoon: from a sequence alignment to a time-scaled phylogeny, and — the actual point — to deciding whether to believe it.

Two datasets that disagree
This is the design. Most practicals hand you one dataset that works, everything succeeds, and you learn nothing about judgement.

Dataset C scores very weak on every R² lookup table you will find — and then returns a textbook pandemic H1N1 rate and a tMRCA matching the published 2009 origin to within weeks.






ImportantThat contradiction is the workshop



Dataset C’s R² is low only because 43 days of sampling gives the regression nothing to lever against. Low R² is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Read the lookup table without asking why, and you throw away a perfectly good analysis.
This is Exercise 9’s lesson from the other direction: there a narrow output is wrong; here a discouraging one is right. Neither number can be read without knowing where it came from.

The optional negative control
A third dataset — real HIV-1 gag from six African countries — is not built by default. Build it with python3 scripts/00a_prepare_hiv.py if you have the source file.
It is the negative control, and it is brutal: unlinked cross-sectional HIV from a mature epidemic has almost no temporal signal (R² ≈ 0.06), because two random subtype-C patients differ by ~0.145 subs/site while 20 years of clock evolution adds only ~0.02. In the HIV dataset, country, year and gene are real; sample identifiers have been re-issued so no patient or study identifier appears. But province, risk_group and subtype are fabricated — they exist so Exercise 13 has something to colour by. Never analyse them as data, and never let them leave the workshop attached to these sequences.
And a phylogenetic cluster is not evidence that one person infected another. Inferred linkage has been misused in criminal prosecutions. That belongs alongside the method, not after it.

title: Day 2 Exercises
section: Exercise 8 — The alignment you did not look at
text:
Exercise 8 — The alignment you did not look at
Session: Principles of Viral Evolution · 13:45 · AliView + RStudio
You have 60 HBV sequences, align them, and open the alignment in AliView. The first and last ~200 columns are ragged and gap-rich. A few sequences have long runs of N. One sequence is 400 bp shorter than everything else.
You are about to hand this to IQ-TREE.

Which of these actually matters?
What do you do first?
What could go wrong?







NoteDiscussion





All of it matters, and none of it will stop the tree from being built. That is the point of this exercise.
Do first: look at it. You already are — that is the exercise. Then trim the ragged ends, because those columns are not homologous; they are where coverage ran out. Decide what to do about the N runs (they are missing data, and a sequence that is 30% N contributes almost nothing but will still be placed on the tree, usually somewhere flattering). Ask why one sequence is short before you keep it.
The circular genome. HBV’s genome is circular, so a linear alignment has an arbitrary breakpoint, and sequences that start at different coordinates will misalign catastrophically at the ends. Confirm every sequence uses the same origin.
What could go wrong: every downstream inference. Tree-building assumes column i is homologous across all sequences. Break that assumption and the tree is still returned, still has branch lengths, and still looks entirely reasonable — see Module 4.
And recombination. HBV recombines. A tree assumes one history for the whole alignment. If part of your alignment has a different history than the rest, no single tree is correct, and the software will not tell you — it will average the conflict into a confident-looking topology. Screen for recombination before you build the tree, not after a reviewer asks.

title: Day 2 Exercises
section: Exercise 9 — A dated tree that is too good
text:
Exercise 9 — A dated tree that is too good
Session: Principles of Phylogenetics & Phylodynamics · 15:30 · IQ-TREE, FigTree, BEAST
You build an ML tree in IQ-TREE, open it in FigTree, and a clade of 12 Botswana sequences has bootstrap 98. Encouraged, you run BEAST on the same alignment with a strict clock and estimate the most recent common ancestor at 1987 (95% HPD: 1985–1989).
Your sequences were all collected in a single year.

What does bootstrap 98 mean here?
Do you believe that date?
What could go wrong?







NoteDiscussion





Bootstrap first. Bootstrap 98 means: resample the alignment columns, rebuild the tree, and this clade reappears 98% of the time. It measures whether your data consistently support the split. It does not measure whether the split is true. A systematic error — misalignment, a recombinant, an unmodelled substitution process — is present in every resample, so it is supported at 98% too. Bootstrap measures precision, not accuracy. Consistent and wrong is an available outcome, and it is the one Exercise 8 sets you up for.
The date: no. Tip-dated molecular clock inference gets its calibration from variation in sampling times. All sequences from one year means there is no temporal signal to estimate a rate from — the rate is coming from your prior, and BEAST will hand back a posterior with a tight, entirely fictional HPD. A narrow credible interval is not evidence; it is what a confident prior looks like after it has been passed through a likelihood that contained no information about the parameter.
Check for temporal signal before you run BEAST — a root-to-tip regression in TempEst. Flat or negative slope means stop.
What else could go wrong: the strict clock assumes one rate across the whole tree — test whether a relaxed clock fits better rather than assuming. And the tree prior is not a formality: a coalescent prior encodes assumptions about population history that will shape your dates.






ImportantThe pattern across both exercises



Bootstrap 98 and an HPD of ±2 years are both narrow outputs. Neither is evidence of correctness. Software reports uncertainty within its assumptions; it has no way to report that the assumptions were wrong.

title: Day 2 Exercises
text:
Wrapping up
Across Day 2, tracking every session:

Two failures came from counting the wrong unit — reads instead of templates (2), cells instead of animals (5).
Two came from trusting an output whose narrowness was manufactured — bootstrap 98 and a 4-year HPD from sequences with no temporal signal (9).
One came from a significant p-value that was a sequencing artefact — caught only by a stress test the binomial never applied (6).
One came from not looking at the input (8).
One came from a result being too satisfying to interrogate (4).
And one — the overlap in Exercise 1 — is uninterpretable without a control, which is the whole of Exercise 2.

Not one of them was an algorithm failing. Every method ran correctly and returned exactly what it was asked for.
And then Exercise 7 turns the whole thing around. Dataset C’s R² of 0.20 says discard this, and the analysis is sound. Dataset A’s tree carries no warning at all, and dates HIV to 1793. A discouraging number is not a verdict, and a confident one is not a licence — you have to know why the number is what it is. Reading either off a lookup table gets you the wrong answer in opposite directions.






ImportantThe point



Day 1 asked whether your question could be answered by your data. Day 2 asks the same question of more sophisticated tools, and the answer is the same: the methods do not know what your samples are, whether your alignment is homologous, whether one base pair of overlap means anything, or that HIV did not exist in 1793. You are the only part of the pipeline that can check.


Bring your own data to the clinic — these questions are more interesting asked of your own analysis than of ours.

Overview
This two-day workshop will prepare you to bring bioinformatics, AI, and data science to bear on real biological questions — and, just as importantly, to recognise when they don’t apply.
We start from first principles: what bioinformatics actually is, what people mean when they say “AI”, what data science adds, and whether you need all three. These are not interchangeable words, and using them precisely is a research skill in itself.
The focus of Day 1 is machine learning applied to real biological data. The focus of Day 2 is discovery and evolution. You will cover biomarker discovery using bulk RNA-Seq, single cell multiome profiling in CD4 T cells, and SIV/HIV integration site profiling. title: 1. What is Bioinformatics?
text: Bioinformatics is what happens when a biological question produces more data than a person can look at.

title: 1. What is Bioinformatics?
text:
Learning objectives

Describe the path from biological sample to analysable data.
Name the major sequencing data formats and what each one holds.
Explain why file size and file shape are different problems.
Recognise that every dataset carries the fingerprints of how it was made.

title: 1. What is Bioinformatics?
text:
A working definition
Bioinformatics is the use of computation to answer biological questions. That is deliberately broad, because the field is broad. In practice it usually means one of three things:

Processing — turning raw instrument output into something interpretable (reads → aligned sequences → variants).
Analysis — asking a question of the processed data (is this variant associated with disease?).
Interpretation — deciding what the answer means biologically, and whether to believe it.

Most training focuses on the middle step. Most mistakes happen in the first and last.

title: 1. What is Bioinformatics?
text:
Where the data comes from
Every dataset in this workshop began as material from a person, a virus, or a culture. The chain looks like this:
sample → extraction → library prep → sequencing → basecalling → reads
Each arrow loses something and adds something. Extraction favours some templates over others. Library prep introduces PCR duplicates and adapter sequence. Basecalling makes probabilistic guesses at each position.






ImportantThe central point of this whole section



By the time data reaches your laptop, it has been transformed five times. Artifacts from any of those steps are indistinguishable from biology unless you know the steps happened.

title: 1. What is Bioinformatics?
text:
The formats you will meet








Format
Holds
Notes




FASTA
Sequences + names
No quality information. Deceptively simple.


FASTQ
Sequences + per-base quality
The raw output of most sequencers.


SAM/BAM
Reads aligned to a reference
BAM is compressed SAM. Needs an index.


VCF
Variants relative to a reference
Positions are 1-based. Meaningless without knowing the reference.


Newick
Tree topology + branch lengths
A tree in a line of text.



A FASTA record:
>hbv_R02B35_consensus
GCTGCTATGCCTCATCTTCTTGTTGGTTCTTCTGGACTATCAAGGTATGTTGCCCGTTTG
A FASTQ record for the same read — same sequence, plus what the machine thought of each base:
@hbv_R02B35_read1
GCTGCTATGCCTCATCTTCTTGTTGGTTCTTCTGGACTATCAAGGTATGT
+
IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIHHHHHGGGGFFFEEDDCCBA@?>=<;:98
That fourth line is the part beginners discard and regret. Each character encodes a Phred score: the machine’s estimate of the probability this base is wrong.






NotePhred scores in one line



Q30 means a 1-in-1,000 chance the base is wrong. Q20 is 1-in-100. Q10 is 1-in-10. The scale is logarithmic, so the difference between Q30 and Q20 is much larger than it looks.

title: 1. What is Bioinformatics?
section: Why “big data” is the wrong frame
text:
Why “big data” is the wrong frame
Sequencing data is large, but size is the least interesting problem. The hard parts are:

Shape — data arrives with samples in columns and features in rows, or the reverse, and nothing tells you which.
Missingness — a blank cell might mean “not measured”, “measured as zero”, or “measured and failed QC”. These demand different handling.
Provenance — the same sample sequenced twice on different runs will not produce identical results.

You will meet all three in the hands-on case study, where a dataset that looks clean turns out to have a fatal design problem that no amount of computation can fix.

title: 1. What is Bioinformatics?
text:
Check yourself

You are given a FASTA file and asked to assess sequencing quality. What do you tell the person who asked?
A collaborator sends a VCF with no reference genome specified. What can you conclude from it?
Why might the same sample yield different variant calls on two runs?

Answers are discussed in the exercise.

title: 3. Where They Meet
text: AI has genuinely changed parts of biology. It has changed other parts not at all. Knowing which is which is a research skill.

title: 3. Where They Meet
text:
Learning objectives

Name problems where AI has produced real biological advances.
Name problems where classical methods remain better.
Apply a short test to decide whether your problem suits an AI approach.
Explain why interpretability matters more in clinical settings.

title: 3. Where They Meet
text:
Where it genuinely worked
Protein structure prediction. AlphaFold changed this field. The problem had the exact properties deep learning needs: a large corpus of solved structures, a well-defined input (sequence) and output (coordinates), and a clear measure of success. Structures that took years now take hours.
Basecalling. Nanopore basecalling is a neural network turning electrical signal into bases. Accuracy improvements here came from better models, not better chemistry.
Variant effect prediction. Predicting whether a missense variant is damaging is now dominated by learned models.
Image-heavy tasks. Cell segmentation, histopathology screening — anywhere the input is pixels.

title: 3. Where They Meet
text:
Where it mostly has not
Small-sample association studies. With 338 participants and 4 groups, a contingency table and Fisher’s exact test are the right tools. A neural network would overfit instantly and tell you less.
Anything where you must explain the answer. If a clinician must act on the output, “the model said so” is not sufficient. A logistic regression with interpretable coefficients may be worth more than an opaque model that scores two points higher.
Problems with a known mechanism. We understand how sequences align. Use the algorithm.
Confounded designs. No model repairs a broken study. This is the lesson of the case study — and it is worth stating plainly: AI cannot fix data that never contained the answer.

title: 3. Where They Meet
text:
A short test
Before reaching for machine learning, ask:

How many examples do I have? Hundreds → classical statistics. Tens of thousands → ML becomes reasonable.
Do I have trustworthy labels? ML inherits every bias in your labels.
Do I need to explain the answer? If yes, weight interpretability heavily.
Is there a known mechanism? If yes, use it.
Would a simple model do? Try it first. It is your baseline, and it is often the winner.







TipAlways fit the simple model first



A logistic regression takes two minutes and gives you a number to beat. If your deep model cannot beat it, that is the finding — and you learned it cheaply.

title: 3. Where They Meet
text:
The honest summary
AI is a set of tools with a specific profile: excellent when you have many examples, a clear objective, and tolerance for opacity. Southern African genomics research frequently has none of those things — cohorts are small, questions are causal, and results inform clinical decisions.
That is not a reason to avoid these methods. It is a reason to use them where they fit, and to be the person in the room who can say why they don’t.






ImportantWhat we want you to leave with



Not “AI is overhyped” and not “AI will solve this”. Both are lazy. The useful position is: this problem has these properties, therefore this method — and being able to defend that sentence.

title: 3. Where They Meet
text:
Check yourself

You have 200 sequenced isolates and want to predict drug resistance from sequence. Neural network or regression? What would you need to change your answer?
Why is interpretability more valuable in a clinic than in a screening pipeline?
Your model beats logistic regression by 1%. Is it better?

Take these into the exercise.

title: Introduction to Bioinformatics & AI
text: Where biological data comes from, what AI actually is, and why the two have converged.

title: Introduction to Bioinformatics & AI
text:
About this section
This opening section builds shared vocabulary before we touch any code. By the end you should be able to say what bioinformatics is, what people mean when they say “AI”, and — importantly — where each one fails.
Nobody here needs prior programming experience. What you do need is a biological question you care about.

title: Introduction to Bioinformatics & AI
text:
What’s in this section




Topic
You will be able to




1
What is Bioinformatics?
Describe how sequence data is produced and what shape it arrives in


2
What is AI?
Distinguish AI, machine learning, and deep learning — and use the terms correctly


3
Where They Meet
Identify which biological problems AI genuinely helps with, and which it doesn’t


✎
Exercise

title: Introduction to Bioinformatics & AI
text:
The through-line
A single claim connects everything in this workshop:






ImportantMethod choice is downstream of data generation



You cannot pick the right analysis until you know how the data was made. A sequencing artifact and a biological signal look identical in a spreadsheet. The difference lives in the wet lab, not the model.


This is why the section on AI comes after the section on where data comes from — and why the hands-on case study spends more time on study design than on the statistical test.

title: Introduction to Bioinformatics & AI
text:
Before you start
Nothing to install for this section. Bring a laptop for the exercise, and a question from your own work — you’ll use it in the exercise.

title: Module 1: Foundations of Machine Learning
text: Before any model: what are you predicting, from what, and how will you know if it worked?

title: Module 1: Foundations of Machine Learning
text:
Learning objectives

Split data into training and test sets, and explain why the split comes first.
Define overfitting and demonstrate it.
Fit a baseline model and use it as the bar to clear.
Choose an evaluation metric appropriate to the class balance.

title: Module 1: Foundations of Machine Learning
text:
The setup
Supervised learning has three pieces: features (what you know), a target (what you want to predict), and a loss (how wrong you were).
Everything else is detail.

title: Module 1: Foundations of Machine Learning
text:
The discipline that matters






ImportantSplit before you look



Hold out a test set at the very beginning, before plotting, before choosing features. Every decision you make while looking at data is a way for the test set to leak into the model.



set.seed(42)
n <- nrow(data)
train_idx <- sample(seq_len(n), size = 0.7 * n)
train <- data[train_idx, ]
test  <- data[-train_idx, ]   # do not touch until the end

With small biological datasets, a single split is noisy. Cross-validation reuses the data more efficiently — but the principle is unchanged: the evaluation data must never inform the model.

title: Module 1: Foundations of Machine Learning
text:
Demonstrating overfitting
Fit models of increasing flexibility and watch training error fall while test error rises. The gap between the two curves is overfitting. Seeing it once is worth more than reading about it ten times.

title: Module 1: Foundations of Machine Learning
text:
Always fit a baseline
Before anything sophisticated, fit the dumbest reasonable model:

Classification → predict the majority class.
Regression → predict the mean.

This is your bar. A model that cannot beat it has taught you something valuable and cheap.

title: Module 1: Foundations of Machine Learning
text:
Picking a metric



Metric
Good for
Fails when




Accuracy
Balanced classes
Classes are imbalanced


Sensitivity
Catching cases
Cost of false alarms is high


Specificity
Ruling out
Missing cases is costly


AUC
Overall ranking
You need a single decision threshold









WarningThe imbalance trap



At 95% negative, predicting “negative” always scores 95% accuracy. Report sensitivity and specificity, and always state the base rate.

title: Module 1: Foundations of Machine Learning
text:
Exercises

Split a dataset 70/30 and fit a majority-class baseline. What accuracy do you get, and what does it tell you about the class balance?
Fit progressively more flexible models and plot training vs test error. Where do the curves diverge?
Construct a case where a 95%-accurate model is useless.

title: Module 1: Foundations of Machine Learning
text:
Takeaways

Split first. Everything else is downstream.
The baseline is the bar.
Choose the metric before you see the results.

title: Module 3: Unsupervised Learning
text: No labels. Looking for structure. The danger is that these methods always find some.

title: Module 3: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Learning objectives

Run k-means and hierarchical clustering, and explain the difference.
Use PCA and read the variance explained.
Interpret a UMAP plot cautiously and correctly.
Test whether apparent structure is real.

title: Module 3: Unsupervised Learning
text:
The core warning






ImportantClustering always returns clusters



Ask k-means for three groups and it returns three groups — from pure noise, every time. The output is not evidence that groups exist.


Always ask: does this structure survive a different method, a different parameter, a resample?

title: Module 3: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Dimensionality reduction
PCA is linear, deterministic, and interpretable. Distances mean something, and variance explained tells you how much you kept. Start here.

pca <- prcomp(mat, scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca)$importance[, 1:5]   # look before plotting

If PC1 explains 4% of variance, your two-dimensional plot is showing you almost nothing.
UMAP is non-linear and excellent at making pretty pictures. It is also easy to over-read:






WarningHow to misread a UMAP




Distances between clusters are not meaningful. Two far-apart blobs are not “more different” than two close ones.
Cluster sizes are not meaningful.
Changing n_neighbors changes the picture. Try several before believing any.

title: Module 3: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Is the structure real?

Different method, same answer? If k-means and hierarchical clustering agree, that is mild evidence.
Stable under resampling? Bootstrap and re-cluster.
Does it correspond to something you did not use? If clusters align with a variable you left out — batch, sex, site — that is the strongest signal. It may also be telling you the structure is technical, not biological.







NoteThe most common finding



Your clusters correspond to sequencing run. That is batch effect, and it is a result worth knowing — just not the one you wanted.

title: Module 3: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Exercises

Run k-means on random noise with k=3. Plot it. What do you see?
Run PCA and report variance explained by PC1–PC2. Is a 2D plot honest here?
Produce UMAPs at n_neighbors = 5, 15, 50. Which is right?
Cluster a real dataset and cross-tabulate against a variable you did not use.

title: Module 3: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Takeaways

These methods cannot fail to produce output. That is the danger.
PCA before UMAP.
Structure that matches an unused variable is your most informative result.

title: Module 5: LLMs in Research
text: Language models are genuinely useful and genuinely dangerous, for the same reason: they produce fluent text regardless of whether it is true.

title: Module 5: LLMs in Research
text:
Learning objectives

Describe what an LLM does, mechanically.
Explain why hallucination is intrinsic, not a bug to be patched.
Use LLMs for tasks where verification is cheap.
State the disclosure obligations that apply to your publications.

title: Module 5: LLMs in Research
text:
What they do
An LLM predicts the next token given previous tokens. Trained on enormous text corpora, this produces something that reads like understanding.
Whether it is understanding is a philosophical question. The practical point is narrower and more important:






ImportantFluency and accuracy are separate



The model optimises for plausible text. Truth is not in the objective function. A confident, well-formatted, entirely fabricated citation is not a malfunction — it is the system working exactly as designed.

title: Module 5: LLMs in Research
text:
Where they help








Task
Why it works
Verify by




Explaining an error message
Common patterns, well represented
Running the fix


Drafting boilerplate code
You read the output
Testing it


Restructuring your prose
You supplied the content
Reading it


Suggesting an approach
You evaluate it
Your own judgement



The pattern: you can check the answer cheaply.

title: Module 5: LLMs in Research
text:
Where they hurt

Citations. Models invent references with plausible authors, journals, and years. Always check every reference exists.
Statistical advice. Confidently wrong about assumptions and study design.
Anything about your specific data. The model has never seen it.
Facts you cannot verify. If checking is as hard as doing, you gained nothing.







WarningNever paste patient data into a public LLM



Sequence data and clinical metadata are governed by your ethics approval and data-sharing agreements. Pasting them into a commercial API is a transfer to a third party. It may breach your approval, and it is not undone by deleting the chat.

title: Module 5: LLMs in Research
text:
Disclosure
Journals increasingly require declaring AI assistance. The rules vary but the principles are stable:

You are the author. You are responsible for every sentence.
An LLM cannot be an author. It cannot take responsibility.
Disclose substantive use in your methods or acknowledgements.
Check the specific journal. Policies differ and change.







NoteA usable standard



Use an LLM where you would be comfortable saying exactly how you used it. If describing it would embarrass you, that is your answer.

title: Module 5: LLMs in Research
text:
Exercises

Ask an LLM for five references on a topic you know well. Check each one exists. Record the hit rate.
Ask it to explain a real error from your own work. Was the fix correct?
Find your target journal’s AI policy. What does it require?
Discussion. Where is the line between an LLM improving your English and writing your paper? Does that line move for a non-native speaker?

title: Module 5: LLMs in Research
text:
Takeaways

Hallucination is intrinsic. Plan for it.
Use them where verification is cheap.
Never paste participant data into a public model.
Disclose, and own every sentence.

title: Machine Learning: Transcriptomic correlates of HIV/SIV rebound
text: Random Forest applied to a real ATI study: can transcriptomic signatures at Week 24 predict which animals rebound after treatment interruption?

title: Machine Learning: Transcriptomic correlates of HIV/SIV rebound
text:
The session
This session works a complete Random Forest pipeline on real RNA-seq data from an analytical treatment interruption (ATI) study. The question is whether gene expression at Week 24 carries a signal that separates animals which rebound from those which do not.

title: Machine Learning: Transcriptomic correlates of HIV/SIV rebound
text:
Materials
 RF_HIV_Rebound_Analysis.R  Expression.csv  Meta_Data.csv
Put all three in the same folder, set that folder as your working directory, and run the script top to bottom.

title: Machine Learning: Transcriptomic correlates of HIV/SIV rebound
text:
The data








File
Shape
Contents




Expression.csv
18,280 genes × 20 samples
Raw RNA-seq counts, genes in rows


Meta_Data.csv
20 samples
SampleID, Status (Rebound / NoRebound), Group, SetVL, and longitudinal plasma viral load from d10.p.t.i to d114.p.t.i









NoteRead the shape before you read the code



18,280 features. 20 samples. Sit with that ratio for a moment — it is the single most important fact about this dataset, and we return to it below.

title: Machine Learning: Transcriptomic correlates of HIV/SIV rebound
text:
What the script does

Setup — installs missing packages defensively, one at a time.
QC and PCA — do the groups separate at all before we model?
Boruta feature selection — an all-relevant wrapper around Random Forest that tests each gene against permuted “shadow” copies of itself.
Random Forest with LOOCV — leave-one-out cross-validation, because with n=20 a held-out test set would be two or three animals.
Ranking and export — candidate biomarkers with scores and p-values.

title: Machine Learning: Transcriptomic correlates of HIV/SIV rebound
text:
Outputs
Everything is written to ./RF_output/:







Output
What it shows

Ranked candidate biomarkers with scores and p-values


Fig1_PCA_QC.pdf
