Fig2_LOOCV_ROC.pdf
Cross-validated discrimination


Fig3_Boruta_Importance.pdf
Which genes survive the shadow test


Fig4_RF_Importance_TopGenes.pdf
Random Forest variable importance


Fig5_Heatmap_TopBiomarkers.pdf
Expression patterns of top hits


Fig6_Boxplots_TopGenes.pdf
Per-gene Rebound vs NoRebound


Genes_Associated_With_Rebound.csv
Directional gene lists


Genes_Associated_With_NoRebound.csv










TipA note on installing Boruta



Boruta ≥ 10.0.0 pulls in a dependency that needs a Rust toolchain to compile. The script handles this — it forces a pre-compiled binary install first, and falls back to Boruta 9.0.0 (no Rust needed) if no binary exists for your platform. If you hit a Rust error, you are running the install by hand rather than letting the script do it.

title: Machine Learning: Transcriptomic correlates of HIV/SIV rebound
text:
The methodological point






Important18,280 features, 20 samples



With far more features than samples, some gene will separate your groups perfectly by chance alone. This is not a flaw in Random Forest — it is a property of the geometry. Any sufficiently flexible model can memorise 20 points.
This is exactly why the script uses Boruta (testing each gene against permuted shadow features, so chance separation has to beat noise) and LOOCV rather than a single train/test split. These are not decoration. They are what stands between a biomarker and an artifact.


Questions worth holding as you work through the outputs:

Does the ROC look too good? With n=20, a near-perfect AUC should raise your eyebrows, not your confidence.
Would the same genes survive on a different 20 animals? That is the question a reviewer will ask, and this design cannot answer it.
What is the base rate? How many of the 20 rebound? If the split is uneven, accuracy is a misleading summary — see Foundations.
Is SetVL doing the work? Check whether your top genes are proxies for set-point viral load rather than independent signal.

title: Machine Learning: Transcriptomic correlates of HIV/SIV rebound
text:
Exercises

Run the script end to end. How many genes does Boruta confirm?
Re-run with a different set.seed(). Do the same genes survive?
Take the top gene and plot it against SetVL. What do you see?
Discussion. You have a ranked biomarker table and an ROC curve. What would you need before publishing these as correlates of rebound?

title: Machine Learning: Transcriptomic correlates of HIV/SIV rebound
text:
Related material

Foundations of Machine Learning — train/test discipline, why a baseline comes first
Supervised Learning — events-per-predictor, confusion matrices
Deep Learning — why n=20 rules out a neural network

title: Module 2: Mapping & Variant Calling
text: Alignment forces every read to a position. Some of those positions are wrong.

title: Module 2: Mapping & Variant Calling
text:
Learning objectives

Explain what a mapper does and where it fails.
Distinguish coverage from depth.
Read a VCF and interpret the key fields.
Explain why HBV’s circular genome complicates mapping.

title: Module 2: Mapping & Variant Calling
text:
What mapping does
A mapper finds the most likely origin of each read in a reference genome. “Most likely” is the operative phrase — it always returns an answer, including for reads that came from somewhere else entirely.
reference  ...GCTGCTATGCCTCATCTTCTTGTTGG...
read              ATGCCTCATGTTCTT
                           ^ mismatch: variant, or error?
That question is what variant calling exists to answer.

title: Module 2: Mapping & Variant Calling
text:
Coverage vs depth
These get used interchangeably and should not be.

Depth at a position = how many reads overlap it.
Coverage = what fraction of the genome has any reads at all.







ImportantMean depth hides everything



“500× mean depth” is compatible with half the genome at zero. Amplicon data is especially prone to this: primer regions get enormous depth, inter-amplicon regions get none. Always plot depth along the genome. The mean is a summary that conceals exactly the problem you need to see.

title: Module 2: Mapping & Variant Calling
text:
Reading a VCF
#CHROM      POS  REF ALT QUAL  INFO
NC_003977.2 1896 G   A   2340  DP=1523;AF=0.98

POS is 1-based, relative to that specific reference. A different reference gives different coordinates for the same biology.
QUAL is confidence the variant is real — not that it matters.
DP is depth. AF is allele frequency.

An AF of 0.98 says nearly all reads carry the variant. An AF of 0.15 says 15% do, which is either a minority variant or an artifact — and telling those apart is the hard part.

title: Module 2: Mapping & Variant Calling
text:
Circular genomes
HBV’s genome is circular, and reference files are linear. A read spanning the artificial breakpoint will fail to map, producing an apparent coverage gap that is purely an artifact of file format.






WarningThe origin artifact



If you see a coverage dip at position 1, suspect the breakpoint before you suspect biology. Handle it by rotating the reference or using a circularity-aware mapper.

title: Module 2: Mapping & Variant Calling
text:
Exercises

Map a workshop FASTQ. What fraction of reads mapped? Where did the rest go?
Plot depth across the genome. Is it uniform? What does that tell you about library prep?
Take a variant at AF=0.15. Real, or artifact? What evidence would decide it?
Compare variant calls at depth thresholds 10 and 100. What changed?

title: Module 2: Mapping & Variant Calling
text:
Takeaways

A mapper always returns an answer. That is not the same as a correct one.
Plot depth; never trust the mean.
Coordinates are meaningless without the reference.

title: Module 4: Phylogenetics
text: A tree is a hypothesis about history. Software will give you one whether or not your data contains any.

title: Module 4: Phylogenetics
text:
Learning objectives

Build a maximum-likelihood tree.
Explain what a bootstrap value does and does not measure.
Choose and justify a substitution model.
Explain why recombination breaks tree-based methods.

title: Module 4: Phylogenetics
text:
The alignment determines everything






ImportantGarbage alignment, garbage tree



Tree-building assumes column i is homologous across all sequences. If the alignment is wrong, every downstream inference is wrong — and the tree will still look perfectly reasonable.
Look at your alignment. Ragged ends and gap-rich columns are where errors live.

title: Module 4: Phylogenetics
text:
Substitution models
Not all changes are equally likely. Transitions outnumber transversions; base composition is uneven; sites evolve at different rates.



Model
Assumes




JC69
All substitutions equal (rarely true)


HKY
Transitions ≠ transversions


GTR
All six rates differ


+G
Rate varies across sites


+I
Some sites invariant



GTR+G is a reasonable default for viral data. Use ModelFinder rather than guessing — and report what you used.

title: Module 4: Phylogenetics
text:
What bootstrap values mean
A bootstrap resamples alignment columns, rebuilds the tree, and asks how often each clade recurs. High values mean the data support this clade consistently.






WarningBootstrap measures consistency, not truth



A bootstrap of 100 on a systematically wrong alignment means the error is consistent. Bootstrap cannot detect bias — only noise.
It also says nothing about whether your model was right, your sampling was representative, or recombination occurred.


Rough reading: >95 strong, 70–95 moderate, <70 do not interpret.

title: Module 4: Phylogenetics
text:
Recombination breaks trees
A tree assumes one history for the whole sequence. A recombinant has two. Forcing it into a single tree produces a topology that is wrong everywhere.






ImportantTest for recombination first



If Module 3 found breakpoints, do not build one tree. Split at the breakpoints and build a tree per segment. Different segments give different — and both correct — topologies.

title: Module 4: Phylogenetics
text:
Trees are not epidemiology
A clade means sequences are similar. It does not mean transmission. Similar viruses cluster for many reasons: shared source, sampling, convergent evolution. Transmission inference needs dates, and usually more.

title: Module 4: Phylogenetics
text:
Exercises

Build a tree with IQ-TREE and 1,000 bootstraps. Which nodes are supported?
Compare JC69 to GTR+G. Does the topology change? Does support?
Take a recombinant, build one tree, then per-segment trees. Compare.
Discussion. Two sequences sit together with bootstrap 99. A colleague concludes direct transmission. What do you say?

title: Module 4: Phylogenetics
text:
Takeaways

Inspect the alignment first.
Bootstrap measures consistency, not correctness.
Test recombination before building a tree.
Clustering is not transmission.

title: Bulk RNA-Seq: DESeq2 and GSEA — Rebound vs NoRebound
text: Differential expression at Week 24, then pathway-level interpretation with GSEA against the MSigDB Hallmark collection.

title: Bulk RNA-Seq: DESeq2 and GSEA — Rebound vs NoRebound
text:
The session
Where the Machine Learning session asks “can we predict rebound?”, this session asks “what is different, and what does it mean biologically?” — differential expression with DESeq2, then GSEA to move from a gene list to pathways.

title: Bulk RNA-Seq: DESeq2 and GSEA — Rebound vs NoRebound
text:
Materials
 Week24_DESeq2_Rebound_vs_NoRebound.R  Organize_Significant_GSEA_Pathways_into_Modules.R  Figures and Interpretation (PPTX)
Data: Expression.csv Meta_Data.csv h.all.v7.0.symbols.gmt.txt
All files go in the same folder; set it as your working directory.

title: Bulk RNA-Seq: DESeq2 and GSEA — Rebound vs NoRebound
text:
The data







File
Contents




Expression.csv
18,285 genes × samples, raw counts


Meta_Data.csv
60 samples across multiple timepoints


h.all.v7.0.symbols.gmt.txt
MSigDB Hallmark gene sets (50 pathways)









NoteThe design choice that matters



The script loads the full expression matrix and metadata as expr_full / meta_full, then subsets to Week 24 only before any analysis. Everything downstream is Week 24.
Status is forced to c("NoRebound", "Rebound") so the DESeq2 contrast is Rebound vs NoRebound. The order is not cosmetic — it sets the sign of every fold change in your results.

title: Bulk RNA-Seq: DESeq2 and GSEA — Rebound vs NoRebound
text:
Reading the direction






ImportantSign convention




positive log2FoldChange = higher in Rebound
negative log2FoldChange = higher in NoRebound

Get this backwards and every biological conclusion inverts. Check it before you interpret anything.

title: Bulk RNA-Seq: DESeq2 and GSEA — Rebound vs NoRebound
text:
What the scripts do
Week24_DESeq2_Rebound_vs_NoRebound.R

Load full data, subset to Week 24.
DESeq2 differential expression, Rebound vs NoRebound.
UMAP — do the groups separate in low dimensions?
Heatmap of significant genes.
Scatter plots.
GSEA against the Hallmark collection.

Organize_Significant_GSEA_Pathways_into_Modules.R
Takes the GSEA output (Week24_DESeq2_output/08_GSEA_Hallmark_Rebound_vs_NoRebound_Week24.csv), filters to nominal p < 0.05, and organises the surviving Hallmark pathways into biological modules — producing module-level and pathway-level CSVs plus dot plots.






WarningNominal p, not adjusted



That filter is nominal p < 0.05, not FDR-adjusted. Across 50 Hallmark pathways you would expect ~2–3 to pass by chance alone. Treat the module grouping as hypothesis generation, and say so when you present it.

title: Bulk RNA-Seq: DESeq2 and GSEA — Rebound vs NoRebound
text:
Questions to hold

Does UMAP separate the groups? If it does not, what does that imply about the differential expression hits? See Unsupervised Learning on over-reading UMAP.
How many genes are significant after FDR? Compare that to the nominal count.
Do the Hallmark pathways tell a coherent story, or a list of unrelated terms? Coherence is weak evidence; incoherence is a warning.
Does anything here overlap the Random Forest biomarkers from the ML session? Agreement between two methods with different assumptions is the strongest signal you can get from one dataset.

title: Bulk RNA-Seq: DESeq2 and GSEA — Rebound vs NoRebound
text:
Exercises

Run the DESeq2 script. How many genes pass FDR < 0.05?
Flip the contrast to NoRebound vs Rebound. Confirm the signs invert as expected.
Run the GSEA organiser. Which modules come out?
Re-run the pathway filter with FDR instead of nominal p. What survives?
Discussion. DESeq2 finds differential genes; Random Forest finds predictive ones. Why are these different questions, and why might the gene lists disagree?

ImportantWhy we teach a broken dataset

The skill worth having is not running a test. It is knowing whether the test means anything. You cannot learn that on clean data.

Participants and faculty, Virus Evolution and Genomics Workshop, Gaborone, September 2025




The Virus Evolution and Genomics Workshop brought together 46 in-person participants from across the African continent. The five-day workshop, aligned with the SANTHE–Gates Foundation collaboration, aimed to enhance regional expertise in viral genomics, phylogenetics, and outbreak investigation.
The workshop served as a platform to harmonize analytical approaches across African research sites, build practical bioinformatics skills, and foster collaborative networks among early-career and senior scientists.






NoteWho was in the room



Participants came from Botswana, Zimbabwe, Uganda, Zambia, Cameroon, Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, and Malawi, with multiple institutions represented in each country.
They included MSc and PhD students, postdoctoral researchers, medical scientists, lecturers, and junior faculty working in virology, bioinformatics, molecular biology, epidemiology, statistics, and public health.





Training was intensive and hands-on, focused on molecular epidemiology, sequence alignment, phylogenetic inference, mutation profiling, and phylogeography — with an emphasis on applying these skills in real-time genomic surveillance and outbreak response.

Important85% end-to-end competency



All participants completed practical workflows in phylogenetics and mutation profiling, with 85% achieving full end-to-end analysis competency using the provided datasets.


Beyond the technical training, the workshop produced several durable outcomes:

Harmonization across SANTHE sites. Participants reached agreement on a shared set of methodologies for phylogenetic analysis, mutation curation, and outbreak data interpretation — expected to improve consistency across African sites, reduce duplication, and increase the impact of local and regional outbreak responses.
A regional viral genomics curriculum was initiated, with lecture slides, tutorials, and datasets archived for future use.
A weekly bioinformatics course was established, providing ongoing guidance, mentorship, and a collaborative analysis platform for participants.
Slack and WhatsApp groups were set up to enable peer engagement and resource sharing beyond the workshop.
New research links formed across institutions in Botswana, Zimbabwe, Uganda, Zambia, Cameroon, Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa.

The workshop reaffirmed SANTHE’s role as a central hub for bioinformatics and viral evolution training in Africa, supporting the Gates Foundation’s broader vision of a connected, resilient African genomics ecosystem. In addition to strengthening technical capacity, it fostered mentorship and scientific relationships by creating opportunities for junior scientists to engage directly with senior researchers and bioinformatics leaders.




An online repository of harmonized tools and tutorials.
Continued mentorship pairing between junior and senior researchers.
An advanced Virus Evolution and Genomics Workshop in 2026, with deeper modules on pathogen evolution.
Expanded funding partnerships to scale harmonized genomic analysis capacity to additional African regions.
